sentence: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, and doctors group it into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
A painless lump or swelling in the neck, armpit or groin is the most common symptom of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, according to the NHS.

sentence: Macmillan adds that a close relative with the condition is a listed factor and that most people who have had these infections will not develop lymphoma.
For Hodgkin lymphoma, NHS 111 Wales says the exact cause is unknown, and it lists past exposure to Epstein-Barr virus as a risk factor.
A GP asks about symptoms and may feel for lumps in the neck, armpit and groin.
If the GP thinks non-Hodgkin lymphoma is possible, the NHS says they refer the person to a specialist at a hospital for tests.
The main test is a biopsy, in which a sample of an affected lymph node is taken and checked for signs of cancer.
NHS 111 Wales says a biopsy is the only way to confirm Hodgkin lymphoma, and that further tests then check how far it has spread.
For follicular lymphoma, Lymphoma Action says diagnosis is by biopsy, followed by staging, which typically uses a CT or PET scan.
For MALT lymphoma, Cancer Research UK says staging usually involves a CT scan, and other staging tests can include a PET-CT scan and a bone marrow test.
note: CRUK MALT page and Lymphoma Action MALT page returned; summary blends them

sentence: For MALT lymphoma that starts in the stomach, a test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria is also part of the work-up.
Because treatment depends on how fast the lymphoma grows, where it is, its type and whether it has spread, the tests that establish these matter for the plan.
The NHS says treatment for non-Hodgkin lymphoma depends on how fast the lymphoma grows, where it is, its type and whether it has spread.
Fast-growing types need treatment straight away, while slow-growing types may sometimes be managed by monitoring.
Common treatments include chemotherapy, radiotherapy and medicines that target cancer cells, including monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab.
Lymphoma Action says active monitoring, also called watch and wait, may be offered for a low-grade (slow-growing) lymphoma that is not causing problems that affect daily life.
For MALT lymphoma, Lymphoma Action lists treating a linked infection, active monitoring, radiotherapy and immunochemotherapy as the main options.
For Hodgkin lymphoma, the Royal Marsden says early-stage disease may be treated with radiotherapy alone or with chemotherapy, while chemotherapy is the main treatment for more widespread disease.
The NHS says targeted medicines or immunotherapy are used if Hodgkin lymphoma comes back or does not respond to treatment.

NHS 111 Wales says brentuximab vedotin is available on the NHS for CD30-positive Hodgkin lymphoma in people who have already had a stem cell transplant using their own cells or cannot have chemotherapy.
For slow-growing nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, the NHS says regular tests monitor the lymphoma and treatment is offered when tests show it is needed.
NHS 111 Wales describes treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma as highly effective and the condition as one of the most easily treated types of cancer.
note: 111 Wales Hodgkin page (page also says most are eventually cured; word avoided here)
